segments.titre: Nvidia, the 'safe' stock hiding unpaid receivables
segments.resume: The video opens by calling Nvidia potentially the most dangerous safe stock in the market. Between 27.8 and 33 billion dollars sit in accounts receivable, meaning chips shipped but not paid for, while some big customers use those chips as collateral for loans they may never repay. One missed payment could decide whether Nvidia keeps climbing or crashes retirements and jobs.
segments.texte: Nvidia might be the most dangerous safe stock in the market right now. You've seen the headlines. You've watched the stock climb. It's a no-brainer. Smart money invested in a safe, cashrich fortress at [music] the perfect time. At least that's what you thought. Right now, the graphics card Titan has somewhere between 27.8 and $33 billion sitting in a column called accounts [music] receivable. That means the chips are built, packaged, and shipped. They just haven't been paid for. And some of Nvidia's biggest customers are using those same chips as collateral for loans they may never be able to repay. Now, one company's next payment or missed payment could decide whether Nvidia keeps climbing or crashes your retirement and costs you your job. This is what happens if the AI bubble bursts.

segments.titre: Sunday night at CoreWeave before the markets open
segments.resume: The scenario starts on a Sunday night, T-minus 12 hours, in the CoreWeave operations center in Livingston, New Jersey. CoreWeave recently went public in an IPO seen as either a triumph or a warning sign, and staff know a worrying number in its financial statements will hit markets in Tokyo, London and New York.
segments.texte: T-minus 12 hours. It's Sunday, 9:47 p.m. in Livingston, New Jersey. The lights are still on in the Cororeweave operation center, which is strange. Sunday nights in the data infrastructure business tend to be quiet. When you're a company that's made it by every public measure, there are automated systems and skeleton crews that keep your machinery humming. Coreweave went public earlier that year. The IPO was, depending on who you asked, a triumph or a warning sign. Investors smiled and clapped as the stock opened on Wall Street. The company was now officially a publicly traded AI infrastructure provider valued in the tens of billions. But the people still at their desks on Sunday night aren't celebrating. They know that in 12 hours the markets in Tokyo, London, and New York will open. And buried inside a core's financial statements is a number that should terrify every Nvidia shareholder. It is public and it's easy to find. [music] And for months, the people who understand what it means have been watching it like a ticking time bomb.

segments.texte: Coreweave's debt to equity ratio sits at 5.27 for the last quarter on record. segments.titre: CoreWeave's origins: from Ethereum mining to AI cloud
segments.resume: CoreWeave was founded in 2017 by three commodities traders and hedge fund people who started as Atlantic Crypto, mining Ethereum with GPUs in a New Jersey garage. When Ethereum changed its model in 2019 they were left with warehouses of GPUs and pivoted to renting compute to AI researchers. Within four years they became the backbone of generative AI and the largest US tech IPO since 2021.
segments.texte: You'd probably assume Coreweave was founded by veteran cloud engineers, maybe former Amazon executives, maybe a group of MIT graduates with a master plan to reinvent data centers. You would be wrong. It was founded in 2017 by three commodities traders, hedge fund people, the kind of people who bought a single GPU in 2016 to experiment with Ethereum mining out of a garage in New Jersey. Their original company was called Atlantic Crypto. And they were good at what they did. They kept buying GPUs and the chips soon paid for themselves at the height of the crypto boom. Then in 2019, Ethereum shifted away from the mining model that had made them all handsomely rich. Almost overnight, Cororeweave was stuck with warehouses full of graphics cards that were becoming worthless for the one thing they bought them to do. So, they [music] pivoted. They looked at what they had. And what they had in abundance was physical machines, power infrastructure, cooling systems, and technical expertise in running dense GPU clusters. They decided to rent it to AI researchers instead. That was the right call. The timing was almost impossibly good. Within 4 years, they went from a crypto mining operation nobody had heard of to the backbone of the generative AI revolution. Soon, they'd become the largest US tech IPO since 2021.

segments.titre: The GPU-collateral borrowing model
segments.resume: The common AI infrastructure model is to borrow billions to buy Nvidia GPUs, rent them to AI companies, and use the same GPUs as collateral for more loans. The GPUs are both the product and the security behind the debt, so everything depends on their value holding and renters paying indefinitely. The H100 sold for about 50,000 dollars at peak scarcity in 2024, a number baked into loan agreements and bank spreadsheets.
segments.texte: The way Coree built itself was not unusual in the AI infrastructure space. That's part of what makes it so alarming. The model you're familiar with today is simple. Borrow billions to buy Nvidia GPUs. Rent those GPUs to AI companies, and then use those very same GPUs as collateral to borrow even more money. The GPUs are both the product and the security behind the debt. That means the entire structure depends on those GPUs continuing to hold their value, and the companies renting them will keep paying indefinitely. Nvidia's H100 GPU, the chip at the center of the story, was selling on the secondary market for around $50,000 at peak scarcity in 2024. That number was embedded into all kinds of loan agreements, leverage ratios, and spreadsheets from every bank that financed the infrastructure buildout.

segments.titre: Customers A and B: 39% of Nvidia's revenue
segments.resume: Two anonymous buyers, labeled customer A and customer B in filings, account for 39% of Nvidia's quarterly revenue. segments.texte: But the people in the Corewave office that night know something else. Nvidia's revenue isn't spread across thousands of customers in a comfortable diversified way. Two anonymous buyers referred to in regulatory filings only as customer A and customer B account for 39% of Nvidia's total quarterly revenue. What does that mean? One of the most valuable companies in the history of the stock market has built its quarterly income around two people who would rather remain nameless. Financially, it's like running a global supermarket chain and discovering that nearly half of your revenue comes from just two families. And now both have suddenly started buying their groceries on borrowed money. Nobody outside Nvidia knows who they are. The company won't say. An Nvidia spokesperson has declined to comment every time the question has been asked.

segments.resume: Analysts guess customers A and B are Taiwanese original design manufacturers such as Quanta Computer, or system integrators like Dell, which assemble servers for data centers. segments.texte: The best guesses among analysts and supply chain reporters point toward Taiwanese original design manufacturers or ODMs. Companies like Quant Computer, which assembles finished server systems and sells them to data centers, or large system integrators like Dell. That distinction matters because it means the concentration risk runs even deeper than it appears. That means that Nvidia doesn't always know or can only estimate who the ultimate end use buyer of its chips actually is. The filing says so explicitly. The chips move through a chain of hands before they arrive at their final destination. A destination that in many cases is a data center owned by a company like Coreweave. Coreweave's entire business model is built on Nvidia chips. Everything from its debt structure to its revenue and existence as a public company hinges [music] on them.

Every analyst on the trading desk in every time zone is going to look at the same sets of numbers that the people in the office have been staring at all weekend. segments.titre: Day one: CoreWeave misses a debt payment
segments.resume: On Monday, markets open calmly until 10:17 a.m., when CoreWeave misses a scheduled debt payment that stalls in interbank settlement and triggers risk-model warnings. CoreWeave's interest payments have tripled to 311 million dollars in a year, and its IPO was cut from 2.7 to 1.5 billion dollars after investors balked at the balance sheet.
segments.texte: Day one. The markets open on Monday at 9:30 a.m. Eastern time. For about 45 minutes, nothing happens. This is pretty normal. The first hour or so of any trading day is often a kind of financial small talk. Prices get adjusted and algorithms recalibrate. It takes some time for the humans to catch up with the machines. Nvidia opens slightly down. Coreweave is flat. The AI sector, broadly speaking, is doing what it's done for most of the past 2 [music] years, quietly inflating. Then at 10:17 a.m. Eastern, a single line item fails to appear in a single bank's clearing system. Coreweave misses a scheduled debt payment. The missed payment doesn't trigger alarms. It's nothing catastrophic. This isn't a company ending default. There's no need to issue a press release or strongarm their CEO into issuing a public statement. A payment that was supposed to clear overnight didn't. Now the payment is sitting somewhere in the interbank settlement system, [music] delayed just long enough for automated risk models to start paying attention. Within minutes, warnings begin to fire through a dozen institutions with exposure to Cororeweave's debt. Those institutions have every reason to be nervous. By the end of its third quarter of operations as a public company, Cororeweave was paying $311 million in interest. That figure had tripled in less than 12 months. The company's IPO, which it originally targeted to raise $2.7 billion, was slashed to 1.5 billion after investors looked at the balance sheet and got cold feet. And that hurt.

segments.titre: Market reaction: CoreWeave -11%, Nvidia -4%
segments.resume: By late morning trading desks know what happened and analyst notes urge hedging. CoreWeave drops 11% before lunch and Nvidia, whose largest cloud customers are also CoreWeave's largest lenders, falls 4% by noon. That wipes roughly 204 to 216 billion dollars from Nvidia's 5 trillion dollar market cap.
segments.texte: By 10:30 a.m., trading desks know what's going on. By 11:00, the first analyst notes are circulating. They're draped in cautious language. Hedge everything kind of pros. It's the financial equivalent of someone quietly skirting to the door at a party where something has or may well soon go very, very wrong. Coreweave drops 11% before lunch. Nvidia, whose largest cloud customers are also Coree's largest lenders, drops 4% by noon. 4% of Nvidia's $5 trillion market capitalization is not a small number. Depending on the exact moment you measure it, it could be between 204 and $216 billion. All of that gone by lunchtime on a Monday.

segments.titre: The market in denial: a contained event
segments.resume: Markets tell themselves CoreWeave is an isolated speed bump in an intact AI boom, too large and strategic to fail, and that someone will step in to restore order. The author points out that this story requires ignoring the GPUs.
segments.texte: At this point, the market is still in denial. The story goes something like this. Cororeweave is just a speed bump, an isolated issue in an AI boom that remains fundamentally intact. After all, the AI buildout is too large, too strategic, and backed by too much capital for one infrastructure company to threaten the entire ecosystem. This is a contained event. These things happen. Someone will step in and order will be restored. The problem with telling yourself that story over and over again is that everyone in the market is simultaneously trying to ignore one other thing, the GPUs.

segments.titre: GPU collateral collapses toward 5,000-10,000 dollars
segments.resume: CoreWeave's loans were written when H100s were worth 50,000 dollars, but secondary-market prices had been sliding as new chips arrived and demand slowed. Estimates now range from 5,000 to 10,000 dollars, about a 90% drop, so the GPUs are worth cents on the dollar. At 2:14 p.m. a private credit firm holding much of the debt starts margin call proceedings.
segments.texte: Coreweave borrowed the money to buy the chips. The chips were collateral. The loans were written when H100 GPUs were worth $50,000 each. But the market has changed. For months, prices in the secondary GPU market had been drifting lower as new chips arrived and demand began to slow. Suddenly, lenders were asking if they had to seize and liquidate the collateral. What were these GPUs actually worth? The estimates being discussed weren't anywhere near $50,000. They were closer to 5,000 or 10,000. That is a 90% drop on loans written at peak prices. [music] A Bitcoin miner who bought his rigs at the top of the 2021 cycle and then tried to sell them in 2022 would have also found themselves in a similar situation. The point is that anything at Nvidia scale is no longer a niche collector's market. The GPUs are the physical backbone of the artificial intelligence revolution [music] and now they're worth cents on the dollar compared to the prices that justified the loans that built the machine's infrastructure. The lenders know this and they have for a while. The question nobody wants to answer out loud is who moves first. At 2:14 p.m. Eastern, a private credit firm that holds a significant portion of Cororeweave's debt instructs its legal team to begin margin call proceedings. The clock already running now begins to accelerate.

segments.titre: Day two: repossession of the New Jersey data center
segments.resume: On Tuesday at 6 a.m., a security guard with a clipboard arrives at the New Jersey data center with instructions from a law firm: the Nvidia H100 racks now belong to the lender and must be cataloged, tagged and prepared for liquidation. Engineers have been scrambling since 4 a.m. to move workloads off, and one compares it to repossession of a house while still moving the furniture.
segments.texte: Day two. It's now Tuesday, 6:00 a.m. at a data center in New Jersey when the phones begin to ring. It's not even sunrise yet. It's a moment not unlike the beginning of many other financial crisis. They're rarely as dramatic as you would expect. Nobody is shouting or hurling insults. There is however a man holding a clipboard in a security uniform. On it are a set of instructions prepared by a law firm that doesn't make mistakes. The instructions say that the company's collateral, specifically the racks of Nvidia H100 GPUs, which have been running AI workloads for the past 18 months are now the property of the lending institution. They will need to be cataloged, tagged, disconnected, and prepared for liquidation. The people at the data center don't fight this. They can't. They have seen the paperwork. They know what's coming. Since 4:00 a.m., engineers have been scrambling to move active workloads off the affected machines before access disappears. One veteran engineer later describes the experience like having someone repossess your house while you're still trying to move the furniture out.

segments.titre: Why removing GPU servers is a military-style logistics job
segments.resume: A loaded H100 server weighs around 400 lb and is wired into the building's power, cooling and networking, so disconnecting it needs careful sequencing and lifting equipment. With about 4,000 servers and rack units costing 30,000 dollars up to 8.8 million for full setups, a third-party asset manager runs a multi-day operation. By 9 a.m. thousands of servers in New Jersey are offline.
segments.texte: Most people have never stopped to think about [music] what this process might actually look like. A GPU server isn't just a laptop. Good luck sticking it in a bag and walking home. An H100 server weighs 36 lb per rack unit. build out a fully loaded Nvidia H100 AI server. We're talking 400 lb of static weight. These machines aren't designed to be moved. They require industrial scale cooling just to stay operational. They're also connected directly into the facility's power and networking systems. The cabling, the conduit, and supporting infrastructure were installed when the building was originally fitted out. To disconnect one, you'd have to power it off, log and tag every component, disconnect fiber and copper in the right sequence, and then you would have to use specialized lifting equipment to move it without destroying the hardware. They're made up of reinforced steel frames and are taller, more rigid, and deeper than your average server rack. Each individual rack unit can cost $30,000 with a fully integrated multiGPU setup costing up to 8.8 million. This particular New Jersey facility has around 4,000 servers or so, which means removing them becomes a multi-day operation that resembles something akin to a military logistics exercise. The lawyers have arranged for a third party asset manager firm to handle the physical side. They have done this before in smaller venues during the cryptomining collapse of 2022. They have the equipment and the manifests, the insurance riders. They are efficient and completely indifferent to what's happening in the building around them. Engineers who built these systems are now watching them get boxed up and prepared for auction. By 9:00 a.m., thousands of servers are offline in New Jersey alone.

segments.titre: Day five: an Austin AI company lays off 35% of staff
segments.resume: On Thursday a midsized Austin AI software company with 400 employees, which raised 200 million dollars in venture capital 18 months earlier, announces a 35% headcount cut. 140 people get calendar invites from HR, many with student loans and recent relocations. The industry had run on high burn rates and patient investors, and the market has now figured it out.
segments.texte: Day five. On Thursday morning, a midsized AI software company at a nondescript tech campus in Austin calls an all hands meeting. They're no different than many companies like them. It felt almost criminal how easy it'd been to raise $200 million in venture capital 18 months ago. All it took was a compelling demo and a revenue growth chart that pointed mostly upward. The meeting is virtual. The company has 400 employees across three time zones. The CEO, who is 37 years old and has built and sold one company before this one, has the look of somebody who hasn't slept. He announces the company is immediately reducing headcount by 35%. Soon 140 people will receive a calendar invite from HR. That's all he can say right now. The legal team has advised and the meeting ends. In a conference room and in home offices and in coffee shops and in parked cars, 140 people open their calendar invites like a death sentence. Many of these are still paying off student loans that they took out to get the degrees that got them hired. Degrees that increasingly are looking less and less relevant or necessary. The AI industry's version of doing fine has always required a certain willingness to not look too closely at the faces behind the revenue numbers, to say nothing of the revenue numbers themselves. The compute costs were high, but demand felt insatiable. The burn rate was high, but there was always another 18 to 24 months of runway. Investors were patient and the models kept improving, and with each breakthrough, the payoff felt closer. For the people who got in early, it felt less like investing in a technology company and more like showing up in California at the start of the gold rush. segments.titre: Why this correction differs: physical infrastructure is hard to unwind
segments.resume: Tech has always been cyclical, with downturns in 2001, 2008 and 2022, and people eventually found new jobs. This time the correction centers on physical assets such as chips, data centers, power contracts and fiber, which are much harder to unwind than SaaS subscriptions. You cannot return 17,000 GPUs to the store or quickly redirect careers built on now-surplus skills.
segments.texte: Everyone in the tech industry knows it has always been cyclic. [music] There have been plenty of downturns before 2001, 2008, 2022. People got laid off, found other jobs eventually. The industry contracts and expands eventually. This time the question is whether eventually has a reliable timeline or whether this particular correction is different in character from the ones that came before. [music] That's because this time the correction centers on the nature of the AI revolution's physical infrastructure. Everything that got built in the boom based on demand that had not yet materialized. Physical things like chips, data centers, power contracts, and fiber optic cables are much harder to unwind than overpriced SAS subscriptions. You just can't turn off a data center. You can't return 17,000 GPUs to the store. And you can't immediately redirect the careers of hundreds of thousands of people who spent the last few years specializing in skills that were until recently in extremely high demand. The 140 people in Austin are right now beginning to find that out.

Alphabet's free cash flow is projected to fall almost 90% to 8.2 billion in 2026, and five tech giants issued 121 billion in bonds in 2025, four times the prior decade's average, so AI is funded on credit, not profits.
segments.texte: And then the data center bill started piling up. All of the money disappeared. [music] In September 2024, Microsoft promised shareholders a $60 billion buyback program. It signaled that the company was flush, confident, [music] and committed to returning cash to the people who owned it. A year later, $57.3 billion of that promise [music] still sits completely untouched. Microsoft didn't change its mind, but every spare dollar was getting redirected into paying for servers, data centers, and AI infrastructure instead. In other words, they wrote the check. They just couldn't afford to cash it. This is what the AI arms race really looks like from the inside. [music] The story being sold is one of a confident sprint into the future. The reality is a scramble to fund it. Companies are being squeezed between investor expectations and the soaring cost of AI infrastructure. For Microsoft, that's led to a $60 billion commitment sitting on the books like an IOU that nobody can collect. segments.titre: Why hallucinations cannot be fixed: next-word prediction
segments.resume: Large language models are poor at looking things up; their mechanism is predicting the most statistically likely next word, with no internal alarm when output stops being true. OpenAI researchers in 2025 concluded hallucinations are mathematically inevitable, since the same mechanism that makes models useful makes them make things up.
segments.texte: Why does this keep happening? [music] Why hasn't it been fixed? Well, because it can't be. Large language models are actually very poor at looking things up. They're not attuned to retrieving facts from [music] specific databases and handing them to you on a platter. Rather, their entire mechanism, start to finish, is to predict the next most statistically likely word based on patterns learned from training data. That's it. When the output stops being true, there's no internal alarm claxons that start blaring. It's rare that your local LLM will humble itself enough to admit [music] that it's actually not really too sure about that fact or how it even got there logically. Their conclusion was that LLM hallucinations were such a big part of how these systems generate [music] text that they had become mathematically inevitable. The same predictive mechanism that makes them useful is the same mechanism that makes them lie. You can't have one without the other.

segments.titre: The brutally honest referee: why trading AI wins and chatbots lose
segments.resume: The compute is the same but the feedback loop is not: when Jane Street's AI is wrong, the market charges it money immediately and the system retrains. AI winners are those with problems where wrong answers are caught fast and cost real money, while enterprise chatbots lack this referee and end up with empty data centers and unpaid energy bills.
segments.texte: The compute is the same. The feedback loop isn't. When Jane Street's AI is wrong, the market tells it immediately and charges it money for the error. Forget 90-day grace periods while customers file a legal complaint. There is absolutely no tribunal ruling on whether the output was misleading in the first place. Wrong is financial loss, potentially financial ruin for some, which triggers [music] instant retraining. The system improves because it can't afford not to. The winners of the AI revolution so far are companies that have found problems where wrong answers are caught fast, [music] cost real money, and force immediate correction. segments.titre: The AI efficiency cover story and the developer layoffs
segments.resume: The narrator argues that the claim AI replaced developers because it is faster and cheaper is a cover story for a corporate panic: big tech took on huge debt for AI buildouts, returns have not materialized, and cost-cutting hits software engineers. The engineers are not just being laid off, the claim goes, the code itself is being damaged in ways that threaten the US economy.
segments.texte: And now everyone can see it. It seems like the AI revolution isn't living up to its hype. In fact, [music] it may be worse. AI is so smart that it's replaced developers. It's faster, cheaper, and more productive. Except that's a lie. AI efficiency is just a convenient cover story for something much darker. A massive multi-billion dollar corporate panic. Big tech took on a mountain of debt to fund their AI buildouts. But the returns haven't materialized. Now with investors breathing down their neck and soaring interest rates, these companies are desperate to cut costs [music] just to keep the lights on. And software engineers are in the firing line. But they aren't just axing jobs. They're destroying the code itself. Software development is being shattered in ways it can't be repaired, and it's about to crash the US economy, taking the rest of the world down with it.

segments.titre: Faster AI code is not better code: churn rate doubles
segments.resume: AI allows code to be produced four to ten times faster, which in theory means more products and higher share prices, but faster is not better. GitClear's analysis of 211 million lines found code churn more than doubled, from about 3.3% in 2021 to 6.87% in 2025, so developers spend more time fixing broken code instead of shipping.
segments.texte: The early promise of AI software development was so impressive that you can't really blame the big tech companies for embracing it at scale. By most estimates, AI allows code to be turned out anywhere from four [music] to 10 times the rate of nonAI coding. In theory, faster output should translate into more products delivered more rapidly. And that means more profits and higher share prices. [music] But faster code doesn't equate to better code. That's precisely where the problem with AI coding efficiency lies. You just need to look at the code churn rates. That's the frequency that code is written, modified, or tossed into the trash. According to Getclear's analysis of 211 million lines of code, the churn rate has more than doubled since the adoption of AI coding began. In 2021, it was roughly 3.3%. [music] In other words, for every 1,000 lines of code written originally, 33 would need to be rewritten or binned somewhere down the line. The more time developers spend fixing broken code, the less time they have to ship new products. Ideally, the turn rate is as close to zero as possible. AI was supposed to be the ultimate cheat code. It would increase output without a spike in costly down the line maintenance. But the opposite has happened. By 2025, code churn had increased to 6.87%.

segments.titre: 45% of AI-generated code introduces security risks
segments.resume: More code written or revised raises maintenance and review costs and brings vulnerabilities. segments.texte: More code is being written or revised, potentially increasing maintenance and review costs, and that brings vulnerabilities. Veraricodes's analysis of between 100 and 150 large language models or LLMs consistently finds that 45% of AI code generation tasks introduce at least one known security risk. In other words, just over half of AI generated code passes even basic security tests. Depending on the programming language and the testing method, that number varies. Java is the weakest performer with a failure rate exceeding 70%. Python performs slightly better but still has a vulnerability rate of around 38%. That might be acceptable if the result is a market ready product being shipped quicker.

segments.resume: The total cost of ownership of AI-assisted software is projected to be 30 to 40% higher by 2027 than traditional development, and GitClear data says maintenance costs could reach four times traditional levels by year two. segments.texte: The total cost of ownership of AI assisted software is significantly higher than what it was supposed to be. A technology touted as a cost cutter has turned out to be a cost multiplier. Fixing twice as many bugs is timeconuming and expensive. That is a huge amount of extra work for the human developers who need to fix the mess. The costs don't outweigh the benefits. It's much harder and it takes longer to fix code once it's been uploaded into the full codebase. If a bug slips into actual production, the problems become even worse. In addition to the extra engineering costs, there's also the possibility of security incidents, compliance fines, and legal issues.

segments.titre: The bottleneck moves to code review; AI creates work for developers
segments.resume: Before AI the bottleneck was code generation; now buggy code clogs review queues, reviewers spend more time per pull request, and savings are burned by review, security and rewrites. AI has not replaced developers but created new demand for them to clean up its mess.
segments.texte: In the preAI era, the main bottleneck in delivering shippable code usually took place at the code generation phase. AI writing code was supposed to fix that. [music] Instead, it just moved the bottleneck further down the line. Because there's so much more buggy code being generated, review cues are clogged. Reviewers are forced to spend more time per poll request to ensure the code actually does what it's supposed to do. And while the generated code is sitting in review cues, companies are bleeding money. Whatever savings were made from faster code generation are burned by the massive growing overhead of reviewing, securing, and constantly rewriting that very code. In the end, somewhat ironically, AI hasn't replaced developers. It has created new demand for them to clean up its mess.

segments.resume: From 2022 to 2025 the tech industry laid off tens of thousands of developers, hitting juniors who did grunt work hardest. The developer layoffs haven't happened uniformly across all tiers of developers. It's the junior developers, the ones who did the grunt work that have been called. Companies were left with a dilemma. Pay an additional $80,000 annual salary or a $100 per month subscription to Claude Max. The companies chose AI over juniors. Data from Signal Fire and Zip Recruiter shows that entry-level tech postings fell by roughly 25 to 35% between 2023 and 2024. Big tech cut new grad hiring around 50% compared to prepandemic levels. In 2024, applications for roles requiring 10 or more years of experience rose by 27% and roles requiring 5 to 10 years of experience rose by 40%. By early 2026, senior job postings were taking up over 41% of the total IT mix, vastly outperforming the overall market. But this sudden job boom is misleading. The rise in tech postings might suggest a hiring recovery or at least that the talent bleed has stopped. But in reality, this is a phantom recovery. There is a senior boom masking a junior

segments.resume: Software teams used to be a pyramid with many juniors at the bottom; now they look like a diamond with few juniors and many mid-level and senior developers. Entry-level job offers often require 2 to 5 years of experience, and the real entry-level market is about 35% smaller than in 2022.

At the bottom, junior developers were hired and trained with some moving up to become mid-level devs and senior positions at the top. Now, it's more like a diamond. There are very few junior devs being hired with mid-level and particularly senior developers becoming an increasingly hot commodity. The very definition of entry level has changed. The term used to refer to recent graduates or those with little to no experience. Today, entry-level job offers often require 2 to 5 years of experience. For real entry-level candidates, it's a tough job market, one that's roughly 35% smaller than in 2022. >> [music]

segments.resume: The market shape inverted because companies need senior developers to find and fix bugs in vulnerable AI-generated code. Juniors once handled boilerplate and pre-review testing; now with 45% of AI code containing flaws, seniors have become well-paid janitors, burnout rises and organizations slow down, wiping out the speed gains.
segments.texte: >> So, why has the market shape inverted? It's a direct response to the buggy and vulnerable AI generated code. The companies that replace their junior devs don't need them to clean up AI's mess. They're desperate for senior developers, specifically the ones who can find and fix the bugs lurking in the code. [music] That's what the senior engineer hiring spree is all about. It's an attempt to fix the mess caused by AI. The junior devs handled the ordinary boilerplate coding. They were responsible for testing and improving the code before even submitting it for review by the senior teammates. That made the senior reviewer's jobs easier. It took less of their time and it allowed them to focus on more highle tasks. Today, with 45% of AI code containing security flaws and twice as much of it needing additional work as before, the role of senior developers has changed. They have become full-time janitors. Very well- paid and highly skilled janitors, but janitors all the same. and it's taking its toll. Burnouts are on the rise. Entire organizations are grinding to a halt, wiping out any theoretical speed gains from replacing the juniors with AI in the first place.

segments.titre: The junior death spiral and the missing future seniors
segments.resume: By cutting entry-level roles, companies destroy their talent pipeline: the only way to gain experience is years of practice, so in two to three years the industry may face a severe shortage of mid-level engineers. If juniors never become seniors, it is unclear where new seniors will come from.
segments.texte: But there's another more alarming consequence for the software development industry, [music] the junior death spiral. By cutting entry-level roles, companies are effectively destroying their future talent pipeline. There was a defined career path. Junior developers worked their way up over the process of years. The only way to get the experience is by putting in the years. Now the chain is broken. In as little as 2 to 3 years, the industry might be staring at a severe shortage of mid-level engineers because they never had the apprenticeship phase of fixing AI mistakes. That creates a worrying paradox. If there aren't any juniors gaining the experience to become seniors, where exactly are all the new seniors supposed to come from?

segments.titre: AI as force multiplier or force divider
segments.resume: Junior developers will not disappear completely; companies that augment juniors with AI rather than replacing them seem to benefit, and for them AI is a force multiplier. For companies hollowed out by AI it is a force divider, with spiraling costs and flat profits.
segments.texte: It's unlikely the role of junior developer will disappear completely. Companies that chose to augment juniors with AI rather than replacing them already seem to be reaping the benefits. For some, AI can be a force multiplier. But those companies that have been hollowed out by AI, it's the opposite. It's a force divider, and now costs are spiraling while profits are flatlining.

segments.titre: The real reason for layoffs: cheap debt, rate hikes and AI buildouts
segments.resume: Developer layoffs are not mainly about AI efficiency. The AI spending boom started in the pre-pandemic cheap money era with near-zero interest rates; big tech piled on debt, hired developers during the pandemic, then inflation led the Fed to raise rates from 0.25% to around 5%, so cheap debt stopped being cheap.
segments.texte: Tech companies thought it was worth the gamble. It might still pay off, but the truth is that the tech companies haven't laid off all those developers because of greatly improved AI efficiency. At least that's not the main reason. The real reason runs much deeper. The AI spending boom started during the preandemic cheap money period with interest rates at near 0%. And the big tech companies piled on cheap debt. They wanted to grow their businesses and fund enormous stock buybacks which pushed their share prices into the stratosphere. During the pandemic, companies like Microsoft and Amazon saw how lockdowns had changed consumer behavior to their benefit. They believed that the future would be more of the same. So they went on a developer hiring spree to start their AI buildouts. The amount required was well beyond their fast growing revenues. So they funded the growth with even more debt. And then the pandemic ended and the bubble well and truly burst. Governments across the world flooded the global economy to compensate for the lack of spending lockdowns. Then it came home to roost in the form of rampant inflation. The Fed had to do something. So, it raised interest rates to slow it down again and again. And before the economy had time to react, interest rates had shot up from 0.25% to around 5%. For the tech companies, all that cheap debt suddenly wasn't cheap anymore.

segments.titre: Off-balance-sheet debt: $1.65 trillion and Enron-style accounting
segments.resume: The big five sit on 1.65 trillion dollars of off-balance-sheet debt, up eightfold since 2022: Meta holds about 420 billion, nearly three times its reported debt, and Oracle's commitments grew 30 times to about 273 billion. Keeping obligations off balance sheets masks leverage and inflates asset prices, which the narrator compares to creative accounting behind Enron.
segments.texte: And that's a huge problem for the big five who are sitting on $1.65 trillion of offbalance sheet debt and growing. You might think that with the cost of servicing the debt much higher, big tech might have scaled back on new investments. They haven't.
